TimeIndex API Reference¶

Back to PlussQit API Reference

This page documents pluss::TimeIndex and pluss::codeh::TimeIndex in the same handwritten style as the Series reference: one method page at a time, with usage-first prose, practical examples, and direct notes about the parts that matter in real time-series code.

What TimeIndex Is¶

TimeIndex is the index-oriented temporal object in PlussQit.

Use it when your timestamps are not just “time values” but the case axis you intend to search, slice, align, resample, and join against.

That is the main difference from Timeline:

  • Timeline is the general temporal payload. It can be scalar or N-D.

  • TimeIndex is the 1D time axis surface. It is where ordered lookup semantics live.

Construction is intentionally routed through pluss::timeindex::make(...) or Timeline::to_timeindex(...), not through public constructors.

Includes¶

#include <pluss/pluss.h>
// or the narrower surface
#include <pluss/codeh/codeh.h>
#include <pluss/codeh/timeindex_factory.h>

Practical Construction Patterns¶

Example 1. Build directly from ISO-like timestamp text.

auto idx = pluss::timeindex::make({
    "2026-01-05T09:00:00Z",
    "2026-01-05T09:15:00Z",
    "2026-01-05T09:45:00Z",
    "2026-01-05T10:05:00Z",
});

Example 2. Start from a Timeline, then promote it into index semantics.

auto axis = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2026-01-05T09:00:00Z",
    "2026-01-05T09:15:00Z",
    "2026-01-05T09:45:00Z",
    "2026-01-05T10:05:00Z",
});

auto idx = pluss::timeindex::make(axis);

Example 3. Build from raw epoch nanoseconds when you already have machine-time data.

std::vector<std::int64_t> ticks{
    1'767'904'800'000'000'000LL,
    1'767'905'700'000'000'000LL,
    1'767'907'500'000'000'000LL,
};

auto idx = pluss::timeindex::make(ticks);

Reading ISO Timestamps: Why T and Z Appear¶

Pluss accepts ISO-8601-style timestamp text, so you will often see forms like:

2026-01-05T09:15:00Z

  • T is the standard separator between the date portion and the time portion.

  • Z means UTC, also called “Zulu” time.

Other suffix styles are also common:

  • 2026-01-05T09:15:00+00:00 Equivalent to UTC, just written as an explicit numeric offset.

  • 2026-01-05T09:15:00-07:00 A timestamp with a negative timezone offset.

  • 2026-01-05 A date-only form. Parsers usually interpret this as midnight for that date.

  • 2026-01-05T09:15:00 A timestamp with no explicit timezone suffix. Whether this is treated as naive or localized depends on the parser and call path, so explicit offsets are safer when timezone correctness matters.

Using This Reference¶

  • Use the left sidebar to open one TimeIndex method page at a time.

  • The first pass focuses on the methods that make TimeIndex different from a generic Timeline: searching, slicing, resampling, rolling windows, and time-aware alignment.

  • If you need broader temporal transforms such as formatting, timezone conversion, or field extraction, start with TimeIndex::timeline and then continue on the returned Timeline.

Coverage¶

The current handwritten pass now covers the canonical TimeIndex surface:

  • introspection and cadence: size, freq, host

  • ordering and uniqueness checks: monotonic predicates, uniqueness predicates

  • extrema and ordering transforms: min, max, sort, unique, argsort

  • positional selection: take, slice_index, head, tail

  • ordered lookup: searchsorted, asof

  • label-based slicing: slice, slice_time

  • set-style axis operations: union_, intersection, difference

  • axis rounding and formatting: floor, ceil, round, normalize, to_note_iso

  • timezone handling: tz_convert, tz_localize

  • resampling primitives: resample_bins, resample_count, resample_sum, resample_mean, resample_agg, resample_ohlc

  • rolling window primitives: rolling_count, rolling_sum, rolling_agg

  • alignment and as-of joins: join_asof, align_union
